opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think most of it remains unresolved, and I'll be upfront that we found learning rate rewinding empirically before we understood it.

The basic observation is this. After you prune a network, you have to retrain it somehow. The standard approach is fine-tuning: you keep training the pruned network at the small, final learning rate. Weight rewinding, which came out of the lottery ticket work, resets the remaining weights to their values from early in training and replays the whole schedule. Learning rate rewinding sits in between. You keep the trained weights but rewind only the learning rate schedule, so the network goes back through that high learning rate phase. That turned out to work about as well as weight rewinding, and often better, which surprised us.

So the obvious question is what the high learning rate phase is actually doing for the pruned network. I have hypotheses, but I don't think we've nailed any of them down.

One story is about optimization geometry. Pruning knocks the network off the low-loss region it was sitting in. At a tiny learning rate, fine-tuning just slides into the nearest nearby minimum, which may be sharp or poorly suited to the new sparse architecture. A large learning rate lets the network move farther and settle somewhere that actually fits the pruned structure. That's consistent with the linear mode connectivity and stability results, but "it explores more" is closer to a description than an explanation.

A second question is how much of this is specific to pruning versus generic retraining. Maybe any perturbation followed by a re-warm of the learning rate helps, and pruning is just one kind of perturbation. You see related effects with warm restarts and cyclic schedules. If that's right, the interesting question isn't really about sparsity at all.

Third, I don't think we understand the interaction with the mask. The mask was chosen by magnitude at the end of training, and then you retrain with a big learning rate. Weights move a lot during that phase. So is the mask still meaningful afterward, or would you get similar results from a fairly different mask? That ties back to the deeper lottery ticket question of how much of the benefit comes from which weights you keep versus their values.

Finally, there's the practical, slightly unsatisfying point that a lot of this is tied to particular schedules, step decay on image classification in particular. Whether the same story holds for modern training setups, with warmup, cosine decay, and very large models, is something I'd want to see tested much more carefully before claiming we understand it.

So my honest answer is that we have a reliable recipe and some reasonable intuitions, but not a mechanistic explanation. I'd love for someone to work out what that high learning rate phase is really fixing.

r001.rationale: The response identifies as unresolved whether a large learning rate moves the pruned network to a different, better-fitting location in the loss landscape.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the empirical finding that learning rate rewinding works well from the still-unknown mechanism explaining why it works.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the deepest unresolved piece is that we still don't have a mechanistic account of *why* it works. We have a very good empirical story. In the work I did with Alex Renda and Michael Carbin, we showed that if you prune a network and then, instead of fine-tuning at the final small learning rate, you rewind the learning rate schedule back to an earlier point and retrain with the weights you've got, you match or beat fine-tuning across basically everything we tried, and you also match weight rewinding, the lottery ticket approach, without needing to have saved the early weights. That's a clean result. But "it works" and "we understand it" are very different things.

So let me lay out the pieces that feel open to me.

The first is disentangling the role of the large learning rate from the role of the schedule. Fine-tuning uses a tiny learning rate, so the pruned network barely moves. Learning rate rewinding uses a big one, so the network can actually escape the region it was in. One hypothesis is that it's purely about step size: pruning kicks you to a worse point in the landscape, and you need big steps to find your way to a good basin again. A competing hypothesis is that it's about the *annealing*, that the gradual decay is what lets you settle into a flat minimum. We never fully pulled those apart. If you ran with a large constant learning rate and then did a sharp cutoff, would you get the same result? My intuition says no, but I don't have a satisfying answer for why.

The second is the relationship to the stability story from the lottery ticket work. We found that for larger networks, you can't rewind weights to initialization, you have to rewind to a little bit into training, and the explanation we landed on was about linear mode connectivity: the network becomes stable to SGD noise after some early period, and once it's stable, the pruned subnetwork trains into the same basin. Learning rate rewinding sidesteps this because you keep the trained weights. But it raises the question of what the trained weights are actually contributing. Are they contributing a good basin, and the high learning rate just lets you re-optimize within it after pruning disturbs it? Or does the high learning rate actually move you to a *different* basin and the weights are mostly contributing a good starting direction? I'd love to see someone do the linear interpolation between the fine-tuned solution and the rewound solution and see whether there's a barrier. I don't think that experiment has been done carefully.

Third, and this is the one I find most nagging: it's genuinely strange that the trained weights of a network that has been pruned by a large fraction are still a good starting point after you rewind the learning rate. If you believe the pruned weights are somehow "wrong" for the sparse architecture, you'd expect retraining from scratch to be competitive, and it isn't. If you believe they're basically right, you'd expect fine-tuning to be enough, and it isn't either. So they're in this middle zone where they encode something useful that's not the final solution. What is that something? My best guess is that it's about the representation of the early layers, the features that are learned early in training and are relatively robust to pruning, but that's a guess, not a result.

Then there's the practical, empirical side that I'd call unresolved rather than mysterious. We showed it on image classification and a bit of machine translation. There's a fair bit of work since then on larger models and on different kinds of sparsity, structured versus unstructured, and the picture gets murkier. With very large pretrained models, you often can't afford to rewind at all because retraining is the expensive thing, so the question becomes whether there's a cheap proxy for what rewinding is doing. And I think there, people have found that the answer is "sometimes," which tells you we don't have a good enough theory to predict in advance.

If I were to compress it: we have a reliable recipe, we have a plausible story about step size and basins, and we have essentially no quantitative theory that would let you predict how far to rewind or how much the improvement should be for a given architecture and sparsity. That gap between a recipe and a theory is where I think the interesting work is. And frankly, it's a microcosm of a lot of deep learning right now. We're very good at finding things that work. We're not yet good at knowing why.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly asks whether the high learning rate moves the pruned network to a different basin or instead lets it re-optimize in the existing one, and says this remains unresolved.

r002.rationale: It separates the empirical finding that learning rate rewinding matches or beats fine-tuning from the unresolved question of why it works, stating that “it works” and “we understand it” are different things.

astra-6.text:
I think the big unresolved question is what part of rewinding is actually doing the work. When we rewind the learning rate, we give the pruned network another opportunity to train at larger learning rates and then decay them again. That works remarkably well, but it doesn’t by itself tell us why.

Is the larger learning rate helping the network move away from a solution that was good before pruning but is no longer good afterward? Is it just that we’re giving the network a better optimization schedule than conventional fine-tuning? And how much of the benefit depends on how long we train?

Those are different explanations, and the empirical result doesn’t cleanly distinguish them. I’d say we have a useful recipe, but we don’t yet have a satisfying account of what pruning does to the optimization problem and why that particular recipe repairs it.

r001.rationale: It asks whether the larger learning rate helps the pruned network move away from its pre-pruning solution, raising whether rewinding changes where the network ends up.

r002.rationale: It says rewinding works remarkably well but that this result does not explain why, distinguishing the demonstrated benefit from its unresolved cause.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big unresolved question is what part of the learning rate schedule is actually doing the work. When we rewind the learning rate after pruning, we’re giving the remaining weights another opportunity to train at a relatively high learning rate and then decay it. Empirically, that works much better than simply fine-tuning at the low learning rate you had at the end of training. But that observation isn’t really an explanation.

Is the higher learning rate helping the network recover from the damage caused by pruning? Is the important thing the amount of training, or the particular trajectory of the learning rate? And why should replaying the original schedule be a good choice for this new, sparse network? I don’t think we have a satisfying account that separates those possibilities and tells us when rewinding should work or what schedule would be optimal.

r001.rationale: The response asks what the learning rate schedule does and whether it helps recover from pruning, but it does not raise whether rewinding leads to different locations in the loss landscape.

r002.rationale: It says rewinding works empirically better than low-rate fine-tuning, then explicitly notes that this observation is not an explanation.
